title: The Sign Code: The Hidden Binary Nature of Deep Networks
abstract: Every neuron in a trained network outputs a number that can be separated into its sign (positive or negative) and its magnitude (absolute size). We call the set of all neuron signs the \textit{sign code}. This raises a key question: does classification depend more on the sign code or on the magnitudes? For overparameterized vision classifiers with sign-preserving activations, the answer is overwhelmingly the sign code. A $k$-nearest neighbor classifier operating only on this binary sign code achieves accuracy comparable to the full model across different architectures, activation functions, and datasets. Moreover, replacing all magnitudes in every layer with random noise while keeping the original signs barely changes residual network performance. In contrast, flipping just 20\% of the signs reduces accuracy to chance. Models generalize well when same-class inputs share similar sign codes. When this overlap is disrupted by a regularizer, training accuracy remains high, but test performance collapses. A margin decomposition helps explain these results: the sign-only contribution to each logit grows as $\sqrt{d}$ in network width, dominating the magnitude residual. The natural unit of analysis for these networks may not be through their continuous weight space but instead through their discrete sign codes.
relevance_reason: This paper reveals that neural network behavior is dominated by binary sign codes rather than continuous magnitudes, which could enable dramatic compression of both the embedding model (600MB) and LLM (1GB) by replacing float weights with binary representations while maintaining performance. This is directly applicable to memory-constrained mobile RAG systems.
key_contribution: Demonstrates that classification in overparameterized networks depends overwhelmingly on the binary signs of neuron activations rather than their magnitudes, enabling potential binary quantization without significant accuracy loss.

title: HydraLLM: Adaptive Width Slicing for Elastic Text and Vision-Language Models
abstract: LLMs and LVLMs are increasingly deployed across heterogeneous hardware, ranging from data-center GPUs to resource-constrained edge devices. Their fixed-size architectures limit the ability to reuse a single model across deployment settings with different compute, latency, and model-size targets. We introduce HydraLLM, an elastic MQA-based architecture. Its number of active attention heads determines the effective widths of the embeddings, attention projections, feed-forward layers, and the output head, forming a nested family of subnetworks within a single parameter set. We introduce a static-to-elastic conversion pipeline that, starting from a pre-trained model checkpoint, includes importance-driven weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with knowledge distillation. We extend this principle to multimodal inference through an elastic projection module whose output width follows the active text width. HydraLLM covers a wider range of active parameter configurations than FFN-only elastic architectures. With 75% of heads active, HydraLLM achieves 2.2 percentage points higher TriviaQA accuracy than a state-of-the-art nested baseline configuration which has 17.25% more parameters. With 50% of heads active, our multimodal model achieves a CLIPScore comparable to that of the 7$\times$ larger Gemma 3 4B model. With only 25% of heads active, HydraLLM increases token-generation throughput by 75.3% over the full-width configuration.
relevance_reason: HydraLLM directly addresses mobile/edge deployment constraints by enabling dynamic model sizing within a single checkpoint, allowing the Qwen2.5-1.5B model to scale down to 25-75% of heads for better memory/latency trade-offs while maintaining strong performance. The 75% throughput improvement at 25% heads could significantly improve response times on iPhone while staying within the 6GB RAM budget.
key_contribution: An elastic architecture that enables a single pre-trained model to operate at multiple width configurations by selectively activating attention heads, achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than fixed-width models through importance-driven weight reordering and subnetwork training.

title: Jev-as-a-Judge for Brazilian Portuguese Information Retrieval: Relevance Assessment and Reranking
abstract: This study investigates Jev, a System One model designed for fast, structured decision-making, in information retrieval. We use Jev-as-a-judge to generate relevance judgments for four Brazilian Portuguese IR collections covering different domains and compare them with the official relevance judgments of each collection. We also evaluate Jev as a reranker. For relevance assessment, exact agreement ranged from 52.9% to 64.9%, while quadratic weighted Cohen's kappa ranged from 0.52 to 0.82. Most disagreements involved adjacent relevance levels, with at least 94.5% of annotations matching exactly or differing by only one relevance level. Despite differences at the individual query--document level, Jev-generated qrels produced similar retrieval system rankings, with Kendall's tau ranging from 0.90 to 0.93 for NormasTCU and Ulysses-RFCorpus across the two evaluation metrics. For reranking, Jev reordered the top 1,000 BM25 candidates for each of the 50 Quati test queries, increasing nDCG@10 from 0.3329 to 0.6331 (+90.2%) and MRR from 0.6852 to 0.9033 (+31.8%). These findings support Jev as a relevance assessor and show improved ranking effectiveness over BM25 in the evaluated reranking setting.
relevance_reason: Jev is a fast, lightweight 'System One' model designed for efficient structured decision-making, making it potentially suitable for on-device reranking. The paper demonstrates substantial retrieval improvements (+90.2% nDCG@10 over BM25) through reranking, which could significantly boost your current 61.4% recall@3 performance.
key_contribution: Introduces Jev as an efficient judge/reranker model that achieves dramatic retrieval improvements (90%+ nDCG gains) while being designed for fast inference as a System One model.

title: SETAREH Transform: A Sorting-Assisted Haar-Wavelet Sparsification Method for Approximate Inner-Product Computation
abstract: Modern deep learning systems increasingly rely on high-dimensional vector operations, in which large input and parameter vectors are repeatedly stored, transferred, and processed. Although substantial research has focused on reducing neural-network model size through pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation, and efficient architectures, the storage, memory-traffic, and communication costs associated with repeatedly presented high-dimensional input vectors remain important practical considerations, particularly in distributed and edge-computing environments. This paper proposes the SETAREH (Sorting-assisted Energy-concentrating Transform for Approximate Representation using Haar wavelets) transform, a Haar-wavelet-based sparsification approach for approximating the inner product between a fixed high-dimensional coefficient vector and successive input vectors. By applying the same sequence of permutations and Haar transforms to both vectors, SETAREH preserves the exact inner product before truncation. It then retains only a subset of the transformed coefficient-input pairs, reducing their representation cost while introducing a controllable approximation error. To evaluate SETAREH, we consider two complementary experimental settings: a synthetic Gaussian-vector baseline and a real apparent-age estimation task using a convolutional neural network on the APPA-REAL dataset. The results show that SETAREH can approximate the evaluated inner products using substantially fewer transformed coefficient-input pairs than the original vector dimension. The findings support its use as a potential structured data-representation method for repeated inner products with fixed weights, while the practical benefit depends on approximation accuracy and the cost of storing or transmitting permutation metadata.
relevance_reason: SETAREH directly addresses a critical bottleneck in mobile RAG systems: reducing memory traffic and storage costs for repeated high-dimensional vector operations during semantic search. The method's ability to approximate inner products with fewer operations while controlling accuracy tradeoff is highly relevant for the embedding comparison phase in retrieval.
key_contribution: A Haar-wavelet sparsification method that reduces storage and computation costs for repeated inner products between fixed high-dimensional vectors (embeddings) and query vectors while preserving controllable approximation accuracy.

title: Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT): Evidence-Based Text Generation via a Closed-Loop Retrieve--Reflect--Revise Pipeline on Edge LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent outputs that lack source support or conflict with local operational constraints. We introduce Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT), a modular architecture that organizes generation as a closed Retrieve--Reflect--Revise loop. SRCoT separates environment state, persistent knowledge, accumulated experience, and short-term memory into provenance-labeled stores. BM25 retrieval supplies local context; subsequent passes expose intermediate drafts, missing-information markers, follow-up queries, and optional claim--evidence mappings. These artifacts inform retrieval, revision, clarification, or abstention decisions. We examine the architecture through qualitative, trace-based case studies in two fully synthetic settings: emergency medical services and Munich-Sim, an emergency-operations simulation. Local prototype runs on an Apple M4-family laptop with 128 GB memory illustrate source-labeled documentation, explicit gap marking, and structured dispatch-style outputs. The traces also reveal provenance-assignment errors, incomplete evidence coverage, and unsafe assumptions that remain possible despite prompting constraints. These cases demonstrate report-level inspectability and local execution, not comparative superiority, hallucination reduction, clinical validity, or operational safety. The architecture separates retrieval and control from the model interface, but behavior across different models remains to be evaluated. SRCoT is a research proof of concept requiring human review, with its principal contribution lying in an inspectable control procedure rather than a new model.
relevance_reason: SRCoT presents a highly relevant iterative RAG architecture that runs locally on edge devices (demonstrated on M4 laptop), directly addressing multi-pass retrieval and generation refinement. The Retrieve-Reflect-Revise loop with explicit gap marking and follow-up queries could significantly improve the current 61.4% recall@3 by enabling the system to identify and address missing information through iterative retrieval.
key_contribution: A modular closed-loop RAG architecture that separates retrieval, reflection, and revision phases with explicit provenance tracking and gap identification, designed for local execution on edge devices.

title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part I: Topology, Input Injection, Recurrent-State Design
abstract: Looped language models reuse physical Transformer blocks across logical depth, but established architectures entangle recurrence placement, input injection, and recurrent state organization. We isolate these axes in models trained from scratch at matched parameter scale, logical depth, and token budgets, and then test whether the resulting design principles transfer to resident- and active-parameter-matched Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. The prelude-recurrent block-coda sandwich architecture consistently improves performance on context extraction and reasoning-intensive tasks. Input injection primarily enhances knowledge retrieval and context utilization, whereas random initialization and separate H/L recurrent states provide mixed or negative returns. Taken together, these results favor the Huginn-style design: at the 730M-parameter and 336B-token scale, the complete Huginn architecture outperforms Ouro across all ten benchmarks. The advantages of Huginn over Ouro transfer to MoE models. At the 8BA0.8B (32BA3B when unrolled) scale trained on 500B tokens, Huginn outperforms Ouro on nearly all benchmarks spanning knowledge, reasoning, and coding, while also exhibiting more balanced expert routing. Under matched training and inference FLOPs, the Huginn-style model uses 75% fewer resident parameters than a 112-layer feedforward MoE baseline. Despite its smaller physical parameters, it outperforms the feedforward baseline on DROP and GSM8K, matches it on MATH500, and remains competitive on the other benchmarks.
relevance_reason: This paper presents a memory-efficient Transformer architecture (Huginn) that achieves competitive performance with 75% fewer resident parameters through block reuse, which is highly relevant for mobile RAG systems constrained by the 6GB RAM budget. The architecture improvements in context extraction and reasoning tasks directly address mobile LLM deployment challenges.
key_contribution: Demonstrates that looped Transformer models with prelude-recurrent-coda sandwich architecture can match larger models' performance while using significantly fewer physical parameters through strategic block reuse.

title: From Relevant Memories to Sufficient Evidence: Rethinking Memory Utilization in LLM Agents
abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM agents to reuse past experiences, yet retrieving relevant memories does not necessarily provide sufficient evidence for answering a query. Essential information may remain fragmented across memory records, obscured by abstraction, or disconnected from the relations required for reasoning. We identify this relevance-sufficiency gap and propose QEMem, a framework that reformulates memory utilization as the construction of query-specific evidence sets, shifting the focus from individual retrieval relevance to collective evidential support. QEMem integrates three complementary mechanisms: query-guided discovery retrieves evidence across multiple memory granularities; source-grounded reification organizes it into structured ViewCards with explicit evidential roles and source references; and sufficiency-guided refinement selectively recovers missing information. Operating on existing memory stores without modifying memory formation, QEMem achieves 91.43% LLM-judge accuracy on LoCoMo with Claude Opus 4.5, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline, MemR$^3$, by 7.6 percentage points and NEMORI by 10.7 points under a shared memory store. Further analyses demonstrate improved evidence coverage and strong performance on questions requiring cross-session evidence integration.
relevance_reason: QEMem addresses a critical gap in RAG systems—retrieving relevant documents doesn't guarantee sufficient evidence for accurate answers. The framework's query-guided multi-granular retrieval and evidence sufficiency assessment could directly improve your 61.4% recall@3 and 67.9% key-fact accuracy on CUAD contracts.
key_contribution: Reformulates memory/document retrieval from individual relevance scoring to constructing query-specific evidence sets with explicit sufficiency checking and cross-document information integration.

title: Noise-shaped Sampling and Annealing for Scalable On-the-edge Training of Binary and Ternary AI Models
abstract: The training loss of binary and ternary neural networks, expanded as a multilinear polynomial over the discrete weights, is structurally equivalent to the energy of a hierarchical high-order Ising model. We exploit this equivalence to apply Ising solvers to discrete-weight network training, while accounting for a fundamental difference in objectives: an Ising solver seeks the ground state of a fixed energy function, whereas training seeks solutions that generalize to unseen data. Our key contribution is $ΣΔ$-Sampler, an optimizer that reconciles these objectives by embedding a stochastic sampling-and-annealing step as a noisy quantizer inside a first-order $ΣΔ$ noise-shaping loop. The loop pushes noise from weight quantization, high-order frustration, and mini-batch sampling out of the low-frequency adaptation band, so that discrete weight updates follow the smooth descent trajectories embedded in the rugged loss landscape. We validate the framework on a planted quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) benchmark with a known minimizer; on CIFAR-10, where a $13$M-parameter ternary model comes within $1\%$ of full-precision accuracy; on ImageNet-1k, where a ternary ResNet-18 comes within $0.4\%$ Top-5 accuracy of a ternary baseline; on class-incremental continual learning, where prior-task accuracy is preserved; and on MatMul-free language models up to $2.7$B parameters, where it outperforms a straight-through-estimator baseline under matched continued pre-training. Compared with standard quantization-aware training, $ΣΔ$-Sampler reduces the training memory footprint by over $50\%$, delivers an order-of-magnitude speed-up, and reduces weight-update memory traffic by four orders of magnitude, making it attractive for on-device training and fine-tuning of large binary and ternary models.
relevance_reason: This paper presents a practical method for training binary/ternary neural networks on-device with 50% memory reduction and significant speedup, which could enable fine-tuning your embedding model or LLM directly on iPhone for domain adaptation to CUAD contracts. The technique is validated on language models up to 2.7B parameters, demonstrating it scales to models larger than your current system.
key_contribution: A noise-shaped sampling optimizer that enables memory-efficient on-device training of binary and ternary neural networks by treating discrete weight optimization as an Ising problem while maintaining generalization through stochastic annealing.

title: When Does Uncertainty Measure RAG Hallucination Risk?
abstract: Uncertainty can measure hallucination risk in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but only when retrieved evidence constrains the answer. When evidence is present, unsupported factual claims become less likely; when retrieval coverage is poor, the model can answer from internal knowledge and assign high probability to unsupported claims. We test this across four instruction-tuned models on HotpotQA and SQuAD. After matching faithful and hallucinated answers within word-count bins, length-only classifiers fall near chance, while perplexity reaches 0.81--0.91 AUROC on targeted unsupported edits. Varying retrieval depth shows why the score changes meaning: detection can weaken with only the top-ranked passage, then recover after adding a second passage. A combined uncertainty and semantic-drift score improves calibration, and measurements remain above chance on RAGTruth QA. Results support a conditional view of uncertainty as a useful measure of RAG hallucination risk.
relevance_reason: This paper provides actionable insights for detecting hallucinations in mobile RAG by using uncertainty metrics (perplexity) that can be computed locally without additional models. The finding that detection effectiveness varies with retrieval depth (number of passages) is directly relevant to optimizing our hybrid retrieval system's trade-offs between accuracy and resource usage.
key_contribution: Demonstrates that uncertainty measures like perplexity effectively detect RAG hallucinations (0.81-0.91 AUROC) when sufficient retrieval context is provided, and that combining uncertainty with semantic drift improves calibration.

title: SAG2: Embedding-Free Multi-Hop Retrieval with BM25 and JEV
abstract: Strong multi-hop retrieval should be practical to deploy without expensive corpus preparation or complex database infrastructure. We present SAG2, an embedding-free retrieval architecture built around a single SQLite database, BM25, and contextual evidence decisions from JEV. SAG2 follows the query-time association principle of SAG (SQL-Retrieval Augmented Generation), while replacing its event-entity and dense indexes with a lexical index over original passages. Selected passages supply terms for further retrieval, and newly retrieved evidence guides subsequent decisions. This moves semantic evidence selection to query time, eliminating offline embedding computation, LLM-based event-entity extraction, and dedicated database servers. The resulting system combines lightweight preparation with strong retrieval accuracy: on 1,000-question subsets of MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and HotpotQA, SAG2 achieves the highest Recall@5 and Recall@10 among the compared methods, with Recall@10 of 86.62%, 97.43%, and 99.00%. It also reaches 81.10% document Recall@10 over the 511,962-document EnterpriseRAG-Bench corpus. Indexing all 11,656 MuSiQue passages takes 2.36 seconds, produces a 25.87 MiB database, and requires no model calls. SAG2 demonstrates that accurate multi-hop evidence retrieval can be supported by compact, rapidly prepared infrastructure, making it a practical foundation for knowledge retrieval applications.
relevance_reason: SAG2's embedding-free approach using only BM25 and SQLite could dramatically reduce the 600MB embedding model footprint while maintaining strong retrieval performance. The 2.36s indexing time and 25.87 MiB database for 11,656 passages demonstrates exceptional efficiency that could free up significant RAM for better LLMs on mobile devices.
key_contribution: An embedding-free multi-hop retrieval system using only BM25 and SQLite that achieves state-of-the-art recall while eliminating the need for dense embeddings and complex infrastructure.

title: Disagreement-Guided Weak-to-Strong Routing
abstract: Small language models are increasingly deployed on edge devices and robotic systems to meet cost and latency constraints, yet their limited capabilities can make reliable deployment challenging. Stronger models can provide assistance when needed, but deciding when to route a weak-model response to a stronger model often relies on signals of response correctness. In open-ended and agentic tasks, however, obtaining such signals can require costly ground-truth supervision that is difficult to obtain at scale. We revisit the foundations of weak-to-strong routing and ask whether routing decisions can instead be guided by signals that do not require ground-truth supervision. We first characterize the optimal weak-to-strong routing policy, while allowing for multiple weak-model responses generated through local inference. Building on this characterization, we derive a principled approximation to the optimal routing based on model-to-model comparison. In particular, we introduce a notion of model disagreement that can be measured directly from model-generated responses, without ground-truth supervision. Importantly, the approximation becomes increasingly accurate as the strong model becomes a better proxy for the ground-truth distribution. Across agentic and single-turn tasks, our approach effectively navigates the trade-off between routing cost and response accuracy without ground-truth supervision. Moreover, even when ground-truth correctness signals are available for training, disagreement-based routing can outperform methods trained directly to predict correctness
relevance_reason: This paper directly addresses a critical challenge for mobile RAG systems: deciding when to route queries from on-device models to stronger models (cloud or larger on-device alternatives) without requiring ground-truth labels. The disagreement-based routing mechanism could significantly improve your system's accuracy-cost tradeoff by intelligently escalating difficult queries.
key_contribution: Introduces a principled weak-to-strong routing approach based on model disagreement that doesn't require ground-truth supervision, using multiple weak-model responses to approximate optimal routing decisions.

title: Embeddings Are Overpriced? A Frozen 16 MB Vocabulary for Small and Ternary Language Models
abstract: In a small language model the vocabulary is the single largest part. In Gemma 3 270M the embedding table holds 168M of 268M parameters, and because quantisation methods leave the embedding in 16-bit, it is also most of the file once the rest of the model is compressed. We ask what that table actually buys. We replace it with one frozen table of 512-bit codes, 16 MB, with no trainable parameters, derived once from a pretrained embedding by principal-component projection and sign binarisation, and we train the same Gemma-shaped body from scratch on the same 2.05B tokens with and without it. The learned table buys 0.20 nats of validation loss for 2.6 times the trainable parameters, but on LAMBADA, HellaSwag and PIQA the frozen-table model is better or tied; only ARC-Easy favours the learned table. With a ternary BitNet b1.58 body the whole model is a 46 MB file, still ties the float model on LAMBADA and PIQA, and on a laptop CPU generates 615 to 740 tokens per second in 62 MB of memory, five to six times the speed of the float model's 8-bit GGUF in llama.cpp at a seventh of the memory. The frozen table wins by 1.7 to 2.3 nats on rare words, accepts 10,000 new words after training with a 3% cost where the learned table collapses by 43%, and all of it is released with the weights, the data and every evaluation answer.
relevance_reason: This paper directly addresses a critical bottleneck in mobile RAG systems: the embedding table size. The frozen 16 MB vocabulary could dramatically reduce the 600 MB EmbeddingGemma footprint while maintaining comparable performance, freeing up ~584 MB for larger retrieval indices or better LLMs.
key_contribution: Replaces learned embedding tables with a frozen 16 MB binary-coded vocabulary derived from PCA projection, achieving comparable downstream task performance while reducing memory by 97% and enabling much faster CPU inference.
